questions.question: What are React components and props?
questions.title: React components and props
questions.direct_answer: A React component is a JavaScript function that returns a UI description. Props are the read-only inputs supplied when that component is rendered. A parent configures a child through props, and the child calculates JSX from them. Components provide composition and reuse; props keep data flow explicit from parent to child.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the learner understands component composition and one-way prop flow.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Treating a component as an HTML template or mutating a prop inside the child.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain values down and events up with a small component boundary.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: A component is a reusable function that returns React elements.
Props are inputs passed from a parent through JSX attributes.
A component must treat its props as read-only.
Different props let one component render different results.
Callbacks passed as props let children report user actions upward.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
A React component is a JavaScript function that describes one part of the interface and returns React elements, usually written with JSX. A small component may describe a button, while a larger one may describe a product list and render other components beneath it. Component names begin with a capital letter in JSX so React can distinguish them from built-in HTML elements such as `button` and `section`.

Props are the inputs a parent supplies through JSX attributes. In `<Avatar name="Mira" size={48} />`, React creates an element whose props contain the string `name` and numeric `size`, then uses those values when it renders `Avatar`. Props can also hold objects, callbacks, and React elements, so one component function can produce different results for different parent-owned data.

A child treats props as read-only snapshots for the current render. It does not edit a passed object or assign a new value to a prop. When the source value changes, its owner renders the child with new props and React calculates the next UI. This one-way flow keeps the source of truth visible and allows render code to stay pure: the same props, state, and context should describe the same JSX.

A callback prop does not make data flow backwards. It is another parent-supplied value that lets the child report an event, while the owner decides whether state changes. Components are most useful when they name a coherent UI responsibility or reusable behaviour; splitting every small wrapper adds contracts without adding clarity. Props make a useful boundary configurable while keeping ownership explicit.

sections.title: Configure a UI building block
sections.content: Component code defines a reusable calculation. Each element created from that component carries a particular set of props, so the same function can describe different cards, rows, or controls without copying its markup and behaviour.

sections.title: Values move down; decisions stay with the owner
sections.content:
Props make dependencies explicit. A child can read a value and use it in JSX, but the parent remains responsible for changing the source value. A callback prop does not reverse data flow; it is simply an input that lets the child notify the owner about an event.

Props are snapshots for a render. When a parent renders a child with new props, React calls that child with a new props object. The child does not edit the earlier snapshot to request change; it invokes an event callback or updates state that it owns.

  B -->|onAdd product.id| C[Click event]
  C --> D[Parent state update]
  D -->|new props| B
```

Boundary to remember
sections.content: Do not copy a prop into state merely so the child can change it. That creates two sources of truth and can leave the copy stale. Keep the value controlled by the parent, or use local state only when the child genuinely owns an independent value.

questions.question: What is the difference between props and state in React?
questions.title: Props versus state
questions.direct_answer: Props are read-only values a component receives from its parent, while state is memory owned by a component and updated through a setter or reducer. Both are render inputs. New props come from a parent render; a state setter queues the owner's next render. Shared state belongs in the nearest common owner.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the learner understands ownership rather than merely calling props external and state internal.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Copying changing props into local state and expecting the copy to stay synchronized.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Use a single-source-of-truth example to show where shared state should live.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Props are supplied by a parent; state is owned by a component.
Both props and state must be treated as immutable snapshots.
Parents change props; state changes through a setter or reducer.
Changing either can lead React to render a component again.
Lift shared state to the closest common parent.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
Props and state are both inputs to a render, but they have different owners. Props are supplied by a parent when it creates a child element. State is memory associated with a component's position in the React tree and is declared with a Hook such as `useState` or `useReducer`. Calling props external and state internal is a useful shortcut, but ownership is the rule that explains how each value should change.

A child reads its props but cannot change them. To request a change, it calls a parent callback and the parent may render a new prop value. A component updates its own state through a setter or reducer, which queues another render with a new state snapshot. Direct mutation of either value bypasses that model and can leave the displayed UI inconsistent with React's known state.

If two children must agree on one value, place the state in their closest common owner and pass each child the needed value and event callback. An accordion can own one `activeId`; each panel receives `isActive` and `onShow` as props. A click reports upward, the parent changes one state value, and both panels receive consistent props on the next render.

`useState(props.name)` uses the prop only when that state is first created; later prop changes do not automatically reset the local copy. That separate timeline is valid for an intentionally independent edit draft, but it needs an explicit reset boundary. Values such as `fullName` that can be calculated from current props and state usually should be derived during render rather than stored again.

beats.cue: Compare props and state by ownership rather than location
beats.spokenText: Props and state are both inputs to a render, but they have different owners. Props are supplied by a parent when it creates a child element. State is memory associated with a component's position in the React tree and is declared with a Hook such as `useState` or `useReducer`. Calling props external and state internal is a useful shortcut, but ownership is the rule that explains how each value should change.

sections.title: Ownership is the useful distinction
sections.content: Calling props external and state internal is only a shortcut. The stronger model asks who owns the value, who is allowed to request changes, and which components need the same source of truth.

sections.title: A copied prop is a second timeline
sections.content:
`const [name, setName] = useState(props.name)` reads `props.name` only for the initial state. A later parent update changes the prop but does not reset that state. The component now has two timelines: the parent's current value and the child's earlier copy.

A local draft can intentionally have a separate timeline—for example, an edit form that saves or cancels. In that case the boundary should be explicit, and a key or a deliberate reset rule can establish when a new editing session begins.

sections.title: Props and state side by side
sections.content:
| Question | Props | State |
|---|---|---|
| Who owns the value? | Usually a parent | This component position |
| How does it change here? | Parent sends a new prop | Setter or reducer queues update |
| May render code mutate it? | No | No |
| Main use | Configure a child | Remember changing UI data |
| Shared by siblings | Pass from common parent | Lift it to common parent |

sections.title: Control sibling panels from one parent state
Boundary to remember
sections.content: State does not have to live at the top of the application. Keep each piece as low as possible while still allowing every component that needs to coordinate to reach its owner. Globalizing all state creates unnecessary coupling.

questions.question: How does the children prop support component composition?
questions.title: Composition with the children prop
questions.direct_answer: When JSX nests content inside a custom component, React passes that nested content through the special `children` prop. A wrapper can render `children` in a chosen place without knowing its details. This composition pattern is ideal for layouts and containers; named props are clearer when several distinct insertion areas need separate meaning.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the learner can use composition instead of building one oversized component or inheritance hierarchy.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Treating children as a single DOM node or using it when named slots would be clearer.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Compare a generic visual shell with a domain-specific component that owns data and behaviour.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Nested JSX becomes the component's `children` prop.
The wrapper chooses where the child content appears.
Children can be text, elements, arrays, or other renderable values.
Composition avoids hard-coding every possible inner component.
Use named props when different content slots need clear roles.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
`children` is the prop React uses for content placed between a custom component's opening and closing tags. In `<Card><Profile /></Card>`, the caller creates the `Profile` element and React includes it in Card's props as `children`. Card can render that value inside its own markup without importing Profile or knowing how Profile is implemented.

Composition lets a reusable component own a shell, layout, or behaviour while each caller supplies its domain content. A `Dialog` can own the dialog heading, close action, and body position. One caller places a confirmation message in that body and another places a sign-in form, so Dialog does not need a new condition or configuration flag for every content type.

Children are not guaranteed to be one DOM node. The value may be text, one element, several elements, a Fragment, or nothing. A normal container should simply place that opaque renderable value. React's `Children` utilities are reserved for cases that genuinely need to inspect or transform the immediate child structure.

When a component needs several independently placed areas, named element props such as `header` and `footer` can make those roles clearer while `children` remains the body. Avoid relying on child order or checking child component types when an explicit contract is simpler. Composition also does not remove accessibility work: a real modal still needs focus management, Escape handling, and focus restoration.

sections.title: The wrapper owns the frame, not the picture
sections.content: A compositional container controls its outer structure and behaviour but leaves the inner subtree to its caller. This separates a reusable visual or behavioural frame from changing domain content.

sections.title: Elements are values that can be passed
sections.content:
The caller creates the nested elements before the wrapper renders them. The wrapper receives those elements as data and returns them in a new position in its own element tree. It does not call child components directly or copy their markup.

Composition usually scales better than configuration props such as `showProfile`, `showForm`, and `messageType`, because the wrapper does not need a new branch for every kind of content. It also avoids inheritance: components combine by nesting and props.

  B --> C[Header slot]
  B --> D[Body renders children]
  B --> E[Close action]
```

Boundary to remember
sections.content: Composition does not remove accessibility work. A production modal also needs focus management, an appropriate modal relationship, Escape handling, and focus restoration. Those behaviours belong in the reusable dialog implementation or a tested primitive.

questions.question: When should you split a React UI into separate components?
questions.title: Choosing useful component boundaries
questions.direct_answer: Split a UI when a part has a clear responsibility, repeats, owns meaningful behaviour, or can be understood and tested as a named unit. Keep tightly connected markup together when extraction would only move a few lines and add prop plumbing. Define component functions at module level so their identity remains stable across parent renders.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the learner can design maintainable component boundaries instead of equating components with arbitrary files.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Creating components for every wrapper or defining a component function during another component's render.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain how boundaries influence ownership, identity, testing, and prop surface area.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Extract a component around a coherent UI responsibility.
Reuse, independent behaviour, and readability are useful signals.
Do not split only to make every JSX block tiny.
Keep state near the smallest owner that needs it.
Define component functions at module level, not inside another component.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
Split a React UI when a region has a coherent responsibility that can be named clearly, not when the file reaches an arbitrary number of lines. Repeated structure, focused interaction, a reusable behaviour pattern, or an independently understandable section are useful signals. A one-off section may still deserve a component when the boundary makes ownership and change easier to understand.

On an order page, a one-off heading can stay inline while a repeated `OrderItem` is a strong component candidate. Each row formats one item, exposes a remove action, and may later own focused quantity controls. The page keeps the order collection, and each row receives a small contract such as `item` and `onRemove` rather than reaching into duplicated state.

Extraction hides internal markup, but every value the region needs now crosses a prop boundary. A large set of unrelated pass-through props can mean the split is in the wrong place. State should remain with the smallest owner that covers every component needing the same truth: local dropdown state may move into the dropdown, while filters needed by a product list must stay above both controls and results.

Define component functions at module level rather than inside another component's render. A nested definition creates a new function identity on each parent render, so React can treat it as a different component type and reset its state. The goal is neither one huge component nor a maze of wrappers, but a tree whose boundaries match clear responsibilities, data ownership, and useful contracts.

beats.cue: Account for state ownership and the cost of a boundary
beats.spokenText: Extraction hides internal markup, but every value the region needs now crosses a prop boundary. A large set of unrelated pass-through props can mean the split is in the wrong place. State should remain with the smallest owner that covers every component needing the same truth: local dropdown state may move into the dropdown, while filters needed by a product list must stay above both controls and results.

beats.cue: Keep component type identity stable between renders
beats.spokenText: Define component functions at module level rather than inside another component's render. A nested definition creates a new function identity on each parent render, so React can treat it as a different component type and reset its state. The goal is neither one huge component nor a maze of wrappers, but a tree whose boundaries match clear responsibilities, data ownership, and useful contracts.
beats.recallRule: Extract a named responsibility with a useful contract, keep state with its real owner, and preserve component identity across renders.

sections.title: Name the responsibility before extracting it
sections.content: A component boundary is an ownership decision. It determines which code changes together, which data crosses a contract, and where state survives. A descriptive responsibility is a better reason than an arbitrary line limit.

sections.title: Every boundary has a prop cost
sections.content:
Extraction hides internal markup, but values used by the extracted region now cross its prop boundary. If ten unrelated values have to pass through, either the boundary is misplaced or the data model lacks a cohesive object. That prop friction is useful design feedback.

Identity is separate from file organization. Moving a top-level component to another file does not by itself reset state. Creating a new component type during every parent render does, because React sees a different function at the same tree position.

sections.title: Signals for keeping or splitting
sections.content:
| Signal | Keep inline | Extract component |
|---|---|---|
| Responsibility | Only part of nearby markup | Has a clear name and purpose |
| Repetition | Appears once and is tiny | Same structure repeats |
| Behaviour | Uses parent's simple flow | Owns focused interaction |
| Inputs | Extraction creates many pass-through props | Contract is small and meaningful |
| Testing | No useful independent behaviour | Unit can be exercised independently |

sections.title: Keep component identity stable
Boundary to remember
sections.content: Do not use extraction to hide unclear data ownership. If two components constantly synchronize duplicate local state, the fix is usually to choose one owner or redesign the state shape, not add another wrapper around them.
